Key findings

  • English has the highest class average (71.1) and Science the lowest (67.4). Math has the widest spread (SD 13.8), so ability in it varies most across the class.
  • Attendance is the strongest single signal in the data: r = 0.94 with overall score, explaining about 89% of the variation. Each extra 10 points of attendance goes with roughly 7.7 more marks.
  • The attendance link is not a fluke of this particular class. Across 10,000 random shuffles of attendance, chance alone never matched r = 0.94 (p < 0.0001), and bootstrap resampling puts the true r between 0.88 and 0.98 with 95% confidence.
  • A randomly selected student has a 33% chance of an A in English but only 13% in Math. 90% of students pass all three subjects.
  • Attendance changes the odds sharply: in the high attendance band, P(at least one A) = 100%; in the low band it is 12%, and P(pass all) falls to 62%.
  • Raw grade vectors are nearly parallel (cosine 0.93 to 1.00), so they cannot separate students. After standardising, similarities span -1.00 to 1.00, and the matched pairs average 0.90, against -0.01 for random pairing.
  • Attendance alone gives an early warning before any exam is marked. Below 70% attendance, a student is more likely than not to need support. Tested on students it had not seen (leave-one-out), the model is right 93% of the time, against 80% for always guessing the majority (AUC 0.97). 8 students are flagged now.
Phase 1 · Python & Analytics

Data setup

The CSV is loaded with Pandas and its columns are checked. Any missing scores are then filled in. The regression method predicts each missing score from the student's other subjects and attendance using least squares (solving Xw ≈ y), so the filled value matches that student's profile instead of the class median.

Statistical inference · Resampling

How sure can we be?

A class of 30 is a small sample, so each figure above would come out a little differently for another class of the same size. Resampling measures how much, using only NumPy and 10,000 repetitions. The bootstrap redraws the class with replacement and recomputes each statistic; the middle 95% of the results is a 95% confidence interval. A permutation test shuffles attendance to break any real link and counts how often chance matches the real correlation; that share is the p-value.

Attendance vs overall score: r = 0.943, 95% CI 0.880 to 0.978, p < 0.0001. Students in the high attendance band average 78.2, against 54.8 in the low band: a gap of 23.4 marks (95% CI 17.3 to 28.8, p < 0.0001). Cohen's d = 3.9, where 0.8 already counts as a large effect.

Proportions use the Wilson score interval instead of p ± 1.96√(p(1−p)/n). The simple formula gives a zero-width interval when every student passes, which overstates the certainty for 30 students:

(p̂ + z²/2n ± z√[p̂(1−p̂)/n + z²/4n²]) / (1 + z²/n),   z = 1.96

The P(A) intervals of all subjects overlap, so with one class of 30 the differences between subjects are suggestive rather than proven.

Phase 4 · Linear Algebra

Study buddy match

Each student becomes a vector v = [Math, Science, English]. Two students are similar when their vectors point the same way:

cos θ = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)

Every pair is computed at once as a matrix product: normalise each row to unit length to get U, and S = U UT is the 30 × 30 similarity matrix. Each score is first converted to a z-score (distance from the class average in standard deviations), because raw scores are all positive and every raw vector points the same way.

Worked example (top pair): Shaurya z = [0.43, 0.42, 1.01], Kriti z = [0.51, 0.34, 0.92] → cos θ = 0.994

Groups are formed greedily: start from the most similar free pair, then add the student closest to the group. A swap-based local search then exchanges members between groups whenever that raises the total within-group similarity.

Phase 5 · Machine learning

Early warning

Attendance is known weeks before results come out, so it can flag students while there is still time to help. A logistic regression, written from scratch, models the chance that a student needs support (overall below 60, or any subject below the pass mark of 40):

P(needs support | x) = 1 / (1 + e−(β0 + β1x))

The weights are fitted by maximum likelihood with Newton's method. Each step solves a linear system with the Hessian, w ← w − H−1g, where H = XTWX + λI and W holds p(1 − p) on its diagonal. A small L2 penalty λ keeps the slope finite if attendance separates the groups perfectly. A second model does the same for at least one A grade.

Each model is validated by leave-one-out cross-validation: it is refitted 30 times, each time without one student, and then predicts that student. The scores below therefore measure performance on unseen students, not on the data the model learned from. The fitted curve crosses 50% at 70% attendance and falls below 20% from 75%, which gives a concrete attendance target.

A correlation does not prove that attendance causes results, and the model learned from one class of 30. Treat a flag as a reason to talk to a student, not as a verdict.

Conclusion

The analysis meets all four phases of the project statement. The data is cleaned and charted (Phase 1); each subject gets descriptive statistics and the attendance link is quantified (Phase 2); empirical probabilities of passing and of an A are computed and checked against a normal model (Phase 3); and every student is placed in a study pair and a study group by cosine similarity of grade vectors (Phase 4). Two extensions go further: resampling puts 95% confidence intervals and p-values on the headline numbers, and a logistic-regression early-warning model (Phase 5) turns attendance into a risk score that can be read weeks before exams. The clearest practical message is that attendance tracks results closely. Students flagged by the risk register are the group to support first, and the peer-mentor pairs offer a direct way to do that.
